body.t: Layers stored in degrees must meet maps drawn in Mercator metres. Convert reference points here to verify your pipeline's reprojection — the
Services returning 'coordinates' in the millions are speaking Mercator. This page translates one pair so the rest of the response makes sense.
Convert two same-sized real features at different latitudes and watch their Mercator sizes diverge — Greenland's famous lie, computed.
Tile servers and WMS services ask for bounding boxes in 3857. Convert your corners here instead of guessing.

Web Mercator's world is a square: x and y both span ±20,037,508 m (half the equator's circumference). A projection that makes the planet a perfect square for tiling — the convenience that conquered the web.

At 85.0511° the y value reaches the square's edge; beyond it, Mercator runs to infinity and the standard simply stops. Polar research uses other projections — this page's cap is the standard's, stated.

popular_table.note: 'Pseudo-Mercator' is the honest nickname: a sphere formula applied to ellipsoidal latitudes. The small lie is standardised, which is why everyone's maps agree.

faq: What does this tool calculate?
The spherical Web Mercator projection: x = R·λ, y = R·ln(tan(π/4 + φ/2)) with R = 6,378,137 m — EPSG:3857 coordinates from WGS84 latitude/longitude.
Which map standard does it use?
EPSG:3857 itself — the web's near-universal projected system.
Can I use this in production GIS?
The formula is the standard's definition — yes for web mapping. Measuring true distances or areas in 3857 is the classic misuse; the projection preserves angles, not sizes.
Which datum do these coordinate tools use?
WGS84, the frame web maps and GPS share — tile and pixel systems on this page are defined over it.
Do more decimal places always mean better accuracy?
No — pixels and tiles quantise the world; extra coordinate decimals beyond the cell size are decoration.
Why not use it for measurements?
Scale inflates with latitude (×1/cos): a 'metre' at 60° is half a ground metre. Convert back to degrees and measure geodesically for truth.
Reverse conversion?
x/y back to lat/lon is a closed-form inverse — the tile and pixel tools in this family expose it where needed.
Datum shifts?
3857 takes WGS84 coordinates as input by definition — no datum shift hides inside it, which is half its charm.
The y at the equator?
Zero — y counts metres-north-of-equator in projection space, growing to ±20,037,508 at the caps.
Print cartography?
Serious print uses considered projections per purpose; 3857 is the web's servant, not cartography's king — a distinction this page respects.
